newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: SPORITELNA NET SEEN RISING, SHARES PRICEY.
newsitem.headline: SPORITELNA NET SEEN RISING, SHARES PRICEY.

text.p: Ceska Sporitelna a.s., the Czech Republic's largest savings bank, expects net profit for 1996 to total 2.1 billion crowns, while gross profit will hit "at least" 6.1 billion, CEO Jaroslav Klapal said on Thursday.
But analysts said questions remained over the bank's murky ownership structure, and the stock was currently overvalued.
Klapal told a news conference he expected the bank would pay a higher dividend in 1996 than its five crown per share dividend for last year, but he did not say by how much.

Sporitelna's 1995 after-tax profit, calculated according to Czech accounting standards, plummetted to 263 million crowns from a previous 980 million crowns after the bank provisioned heavily for risky loans.

The bank's 1995 gross profit was 9.17 billion crowns but it assigned almost an identical sum, 9.13 billion, to its reserves covering "classified" loans -- those whose likelihood of recovery ranges from doubtful to hopeless.
Sporitelna, which is 45 percent state-owned, has been plagued by bad debts since soon after the 1989 fall of Communism.
At the time, the government put pressure on most Czech banks to lend to the new class of entrepreneurs. Since then risk assessment has been tightened up as Czech banking expertise has improved.

Eventhough analysts agreed that the financial situation of the bank was markedly better this year than it was last year, they said shares of the bank -- which rose 16 crowns to 351 crowns on Thursday, were overvalued.

Analysts say they are closely watching what appears to be a strong acquisition of shares in Sporitelna by the usually secretive Czech investment group Motoinvest and the rival bank Investicni a Postovni Banka a.s.
"The attractiveness of (Sporitelna) could greatly drop if Motoinvest took a more significant share in management," said Richard Podpiera analyst at the investment house Atlantk FT.

"The fate of banking institutions is a sensitive political question, that's why the state wouldn't allow Motoinvest, as a not-too-transparent financial group, to take control for at least the next two or three years."

Sporitelna has declined repeated requests to publish their current shareholder structure. The state-run National Property Fund reports it holds 45 percent, while Motoinvest earlier this summer said it had roughly 10 percent.
The holdings of other Sporitelna shareholders -- IPB, Komercni Banka , and the Czech bank Ceskoslovenska Obchodni Banka, have not been specified.

"Considering the stucture of owners, and its unfinished privatisation, I expect it's possible the (Sporitelna) share price will fluctuate for a fairly long term above its intrinsic value," said analyst Pavel Sobisek of Zivnostensa Banka.
